A 38-year-old man who sustained a severe head injury several months ago undergoes evaluation of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis function.  He receives a single dose of metyrapone, after which serial blood samples are obtained to measure serum 11-deoxycortisol.  Results are shown below.

An increase in which of the following is most directly responsible for the finding observed in the graph?​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​
explanation:
This patient underwent a metyrapone stimulation test to evaluate the integrity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which may be disrupted by head trauma (eg, injury to the pituitary or pituitary stalk).

Cortisol secretion is governed by a negative feedback loop.  Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) is secreted by the hypothalamus in response to stress and circadian signals; CRH stimulates ACTH release from the anterior pituitary, which in turn drives cortisol synthesis in the adrenal zona fasciculata.  High cortisol levels then lead to suppression of CRH and ACTH secretion.

Metyrapone blocks cortisol synthesis by inhibiting 11β-hydroxylase, which converts 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol (Choice B).  Because 11-deoxycortisol lacks glucocorticoid activity, it does not provide feedback inhibition to the hypothalamus or pituitary.  As a result, the reduction in cortisol levels following metyrapone administration causes an increase in ACTH secretion.  This stimulates adrenal steroidogenesis, but the enzymatic blockade leads to accumulation of 11-deoxycortisol (as seen in this patient), which is further metabolized by the liver to 17-hydroxycorticosteroids that accumulate in the urine.

Failure of 11-deoxycortisol to rise after metyrapone indicates adrenal insufficiency.  With pituitary or hypothalamic dysfunction, ACTH cannot increase, so steroidogenesis is never stimulated; with primary adrenal disease, ACTH rises appropriately but the dysfunctional cortex cannot generate steroid precursors.  Therefore, primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency can be distinguished based on plasma ACTH levels.

(Choice A)  Adrenal androgen production increases after metyrapone administration because the increase in ACTH stimulates steroidogenesis throughout the ACTH-responsive cortex, including the zona reticularis.  The resulting pathway acceleration increases production of 17-hydroxyprogesterone, which is shunted toward androgen synthesis (the same diversion that causes virilization in 21-hydroxylase and 11β-hydroxylase deficiencies).  However, the increase in androgen production is a parallel consequence of the ACTH surge rather than the cause of the rise in 11-deoxycortisol.

(Choices C and E)  Aldosterone synthesis in the zona glomerulosa requires 11β-hydroxylase, so metyrapone decreases (rather than increases) aldosterone production.  However, the accumulating precursor 11-deoxycorticosterone is itself a mineralocorticoid, which prevents overt mineralocorticoid deficiency; renin levels therefore do not change significantly.

Educational objective:Cortisol negatively regulates its own production at the level of the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary.  Metyrapone inhibits 11β-hydroxylase, interrupting the conversion of 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol.  In patients with an intact hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, the loss of cortisol-mediated negative feedback leads to an increase in ACTH, which raises serum 11-deoxycortisol levels.​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​
